statement: For a substring-based line-scan Validator (not an AST visitor), the mem-arc-06-0002 double-dispatch gotcha shows up as SUBSTRING containment rather than double node-visits: a marker like `eval(` also matches inside `ast.literal_eval(`, and `print(` also matches inside a hypothetical `pprint(`. A plain `str::contains` guard is blind to this; it needs a word-boundary check (the byte before the match must not be an identifier character) or the pass fixture will spuriously trip the rule.
why: Discovered live: enforcer-lang-py's PY-4.16 (ban eval/exec/compile) fired on its own PASS fixture because the pass fixture legitimately used `ast.literal_eval(expr)` as the SAFE alternative to `eval(expr)` -- exactly the kind of pass fixture a real rule author would write, and exactly the kind of match a careless substring scan gets wrong.
howToApply: Any enforcer-lang-* crate building line/substring-scan validators (not full AST) for a banned-call-name rule should word-boundary-guard the marker (reject a match immediately preceded by [A-Za-z0-9_]), not just guard against comments/strings. enforcer-lang-py's crates/enforcer-lang-py/src/line_marker.rs Guard::WordBoundary + contains_at_word_boundary is a reusable pattern for this.

statement: A `LineStartsWith` prefix guard is not sufficient to distinguish a WEAK bare-truthiness assertion (`assert user`) from a STRONG concrete assertion (`assert user.name == "alice"`) when the weak form's marker text is a literal prefix of the strong form's text -- `"assert user"` matches both lines under `starts_with`. The fix is not a smarter marker string, it is checking the ENTIRE remainder after `assert ` is exactly one of the known bare identifiers, not merely a prefix match.
why: enforcer-lang-py's PY-6.2 (weak-assertions) pass fixture `assert user.name == "alice"` tripped the rule under a naive `LineStartsWith("assert user")` marker, because `starts_with` doesn't care what follows. This is a second flavor of the mem-arc-06-0002 family: guarding POSITION (line start) is not the same as guarding SHAPE (the whole statement, not just its prefix).
howToApply: When a rule's fail/pass distinction hinges on "this identifier appears ALONE" vs "this identifier is the head of a longer expression", write a dedicated exact-remainder check (see crates/enforcer-lang-py/src/line_marker.rs WeakAssertionValidator: strips the `assert ` prefix, then requires the REST to equal a known identifier exactly) rather than trying to express it as a marker string plus a Guard variant.

statement: The legacy `required-tests` check (rule TEST-2.2) flags Rust's idiomatic `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { ... }` inline-test convention as "contains inline test code; move it under an organized test root" -- a false positive for every Rust crate in this workspace (confirmed also present in crates/enforcer-validator and crates/enforcer-rules, not just enforcer-lang-py), since Rust's convention IS inline `#[cfg(test)]`, not a separate test-root directory like the legacy JS/TS codebase used.
why: Dogfooding `ocentra_enforcer_check --check required-tests` on crates/enforcer-lang-py/src/{lib.rs,line_marker.rs} surfaced 2 TEST-2.2 findings purely for using `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`, which is correct Rust, not a defect. Spawned task_94e15358 (scope TEST-2.2 to recognize `#[cfg(test)]` as compliant for `.rs` files) rather than distorting the crate's structure to satisfy a JS-oriented rule.
howToApply: Any future enforcer-lang-* crate author dogfooding `required-tests`/TEST-2.2 on their own `.rs` files should expect this false positive on ordinary `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` blocks; do not move Rust unit tests out of the file to satisfy it -- file/spawn a task against TEST-2.2's rule scope instead (this is the RR-6.1-shaped class of gap the protocol already flags as verbatim-summarized/count-only).
